hook: What an *API* actually is, explained without the jargon

points.title: A menu for software
points.body: An API lists what a program can do for you, and how to ask.

points.title: You send a request
points.body: Your app asks for something specific, like a user's profile or today's orders.

points.title: You get a response
points.body: The other system replies with data, usually as JSON, or an error explaining why.

cta: Which concept should I *explain* next?
caption:
APIs sound complicated until you picture them as a menu.
Request in, response out. That is the whole idea.
What should I break down next? 👇

hook: Validate your SaaS idea *before* you write any code

points.title: Talk to ten real users
points.body: Ask about their current workflow and pain, not whether they like your idea.

points.title: Look for money already spent
points.body: If people pay for clunky workarounds today, the problem is real enough.

points.title: Sell it before building it
points.body: A landing page with a waitlist or preorder tests demand in days, not months.

cta: How did you *validate* your last idea?
caption:
Code is the most expensive way to test an idea.
Conversations and a landing page are much cheaper.
How do you validate before building? 👇

hook: A simple *two-list* system for focused dev days

points.title: List one: today's three tasks
points.body: Pick only three outcomes you will finish today. Everything else waits.

points.title: List two: the parking lot
points.body: New ideas and requests go here instead of breaking your current focus.

points.title: Review both every evening
points.body: Five minutes moving items between lists keeps tomorrow ready to start.

cta: What keeps *you* focused during deep work?
caption:
Most focus problems are really list problems.
Three tasks for today, everything else parked.
What keeps you focused? 👇

hook: Use AI coding assistants like a *senior reviewer*, not autocomplete

points.title: Ask for a review first
points.body: Paste your diff and ask what could break. It catches missed edge cases.

points.title: Give it real context
points.body: Share types, error messages and constraints. Vague prompts produce confident, wrong code.

points.title: Verify everything it writes
points.body: Run the tests and read each line. You still own what ships.

cta: How do you *use* AI in your workflow?
caption:
AI is most useful when it questions your code, not just writes it.
Context in, careful review out.
How do you use AI while coding? 👇

hook: Stop trusting *TypeScript types* for data from outside your app

points.title: Types vanish at runtime
points.body: TypeScript checks your code at build time. It cannot check API responses.

points.title: Validate at the boundary
points.body: Parse external data with a schema library like Zod before using it.

points.title: Infer types from the schema
points.body: One schema gives you runtime checks and static types that never drift apart.

cta: Do you *validate* your API responses?
caption:
Types describe what you expect, not what you receive.
Validate at the edges and trust the types inside.
Do you validate external data? 👇

hook: Clean code matters less than *shipping* something people actually use

points.title: Users never see your code
points.body: They see speed, bugs and whether it solves their problem.

points.title: Perfect code can wait
points.body: Refactoring a product with users beats polishing one nobody has tried.

points.title: But do not skip basics
points.body: Tests for critical paths and readable names save you when it grows.

cta: Do you *agree* or disagree with this?
caption:
Clean code is a tool, not the goal.
Ship first, then improve what real users touch.
Agree or disagree? 👇

hook: Write *fixed-scope* proposals so projects do not quietly grow forever

points.title: List every deliverable
points.body: Spell out exactly what is included, page by page or feature by feature.

points.title: Name what is excluded
points.body: Saying what is out of scope prevents most arguments later.

points.title: Price changes separately
points.body: New requests become a small change order, not free extra work.

cta: How do you *handle* scope creep?
caption:
Scope creep usually starts with a vague proposal.
Clear deliverables and exclusions protect both sides.
How do you handle it? 👇

hook: What *caching* really means, in under thirty seconds

points.title: Keep a nearby copy
points.body: A cache stores results you already fetched so you can reuse them quickly.

points.title: Faster and cheaper
points.body: Fewer database or API calls means quicker pages and lower server costs.

points.title: The hard part: staleness
points.body: Cached data can be outdated, so you decide when to refresh or invalidate it.

cta: What *concept* confuses you most right now?
caption:
Caching is just keeping a copy close by.
The tricky part is knowing when that copy is too old.
What should I explain next? 👇

hook: Your first SaaS version needs *fewer features* than you think

points.title: Solve one painful problem
points.body: Pick the single job users would pay for and do it well.

points.title: Skip the admin dashboard
points.body: Early on, manual work behind the scenes is fine. Automate once it hurts.

points.title: Charge from day one
points.body: Payment is the clearest signal that you built something people want.

cta: What would you *cut* from your MVP?
caption:
Every extra feature delays the moment you learn something.
One painful problem, solved well, is enough to start.
What would you cut? 👇

hook: Write the *next step* down before you close your laptop

points.title: Stopping mid-task costs focus
points.body: Tomorrow you spend time remembering where you were and what came next.

points.title: Leave a clear note
points.body: One line: the next file, function or command you were about to run.

points.title: Start fast the next day
points.body: Reading one line gets you back into flow in minutes, not an hour.

cta: How do you *restart* after a break?
caption:
The hardest part of coding is often getting started again.
A one-line note fixes that.
How do you get back into flow? 👇

hook: Three ways to get *better answers* from AI coding tools

points.title: Show the exact error
points.body: Paste the full error message and stack trace, not a paraphrase of it.

points.title: Share the relevant code
points.body: Include the function, its types and how it is called. Context beats cleverness.

points.title: Ask for options, not answers
points.body: Request two approaches with tradeoffs, then choose the one that fits your project.

cta: Which AI coding tool do you *use* daily?
caption:
Better input gets better code from any AI tool.
Errors, context and tradeoffs make the difference.
Which tool do you use? 👇

hook: Add *indexes* for the columns your queries filter on most

points.title: Slow queries often scan everything
points.body: Without an index, Postgres may read every row to find a few matches.

points.title: Index what you filter on
points.body: Columns used in WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY are the usual candidates.

points.title: Check with EXPLAIN ANALYZE
points.body: It shows whether Postgres used your index and where time actually went.

cta: Have you ever *checked* your query plans?
caption:
A slow page is often one missing index.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows you exactly where the time goes.
Have you tried it? 👇

hook: Learning a new framework every month is *slowing* you down

points.title: Depth beats breadth
points.body: Knowing one stack well lets you ship faster and debug with confidence.

points.title: Fundamentals transfer
points.body: HTTP, databases and JavaScript itself outlast any framework you learn this year.

points.title: Learn new tools on purpose
points.body: Pick one up when a real project needs it, not because it trends.

cta: Are you learning a new *framework* right now?
caption:
Chasing every new framework feels productive but rarely is.
Go deep on one stack and the fundamentals.
What are you learning now? 👇

hook: Reply to clients *fast*, even when you do not have the answer

points.title: Speed builds trust
points.body: A quick reply tells clients their project is in safe hands.

points.title: Acknowledge, then give a time
points.body: Say you received it and when they will hear back with details.

points.title: Keep that promise
points.body: Replying when you said you would matters more than replying instantly.

cta: How fast do you *reply* to clients?
caption:
Silence makes clients nervous, even when work is on track.
A quick acknowledgement with a time fixes that.
How fast do you reply? 👇

hook: A *webhook* is just an app calling you back

points.title: Polling asks again and again
points.body: Without webhooks, your app keeps asking another service whether anything has changed yet.

points.title: A webhook pushes the news to you
points.body: The other service sends a request to your URL the moment something happens.

points.title: Verify it, then answer quickly
points.body: Check the signature so you know it is real, reply fast, and expect repeat deliveries.

cta: Which *service* sends you webhooks most?
caption:
Webhooks sound scary but the idea is simple.
They are the internet's way of saying: don't call us, we'll call you.
Have you ever debugged a webhook that never arrived? 👇

hook: Ask what people do *today* about the problem

points.title: Skip asking if they would use it
points.body: People say yes to be polite. Ask what they already do about the problem.

points.title: Look for a messy workaround
points.body: Spreadsheets, copy and paste, and manual reminders all show the problem is real.

points.title: Ask what the last time cost them
points.body: Time lost or money spent tells you how much the problem actually hurts.

cta: What *workaround* have you seen lately?
caption:
Good ideas often hide inside ugly workarounds.
Find the spreadsheet before you build the app.
What is the messiest workflow you have seen? 👇

hook: Put a *timer* on every bug you get stuck on

points.title: Pick a limit before you start
points.body: Decide how long you will struggle alone, like thirty minutes, and set a timer.

points.title: Write down what you already tried
points.body: Notes stop you repeating failed fixes and make asking for help much easier.

points.title: When time is up, change approach
points.body: Ask someone, search differently, or take a walk. Do not keep looping the same idea.

cta: How long do you *struggle* before asking?
caption:
Being stuck is normal. Being stuck for hours with no plan is optional.
A timer turns frustration into a decision.
How long is your limit? 👇

hook: Ask AI to *explain* code before it changes anything

points.title: Paste the code and ask for a summary
points.body: Have the assistant describe what the code does in plain words first.

points.title: Compare it to your own understanding
points.body: If its summary is wrong, it will likely write a wrong change too.

points.title: Only then ask for the edit
points.body: Request a small, specific change and read the result before you accept it.

cta: Do you *review* AI code line by line?
caption:
Explaining first catches misunderstandings before they become bugs.
It also helps you learn unfamiliar code faster.
Do you ask AI to explain before it edits? 👇

hook: Keep your Next.js components on the *server* by default

points.title: Server components send less JavaScript
points.body: They render on the server, so the browser has less code to download and run.

points.title: Add use client only when needed
points.body: Reach for it when you need state, effects, or browser events like clicks.

points.title: Push client code to small leaves
points.body: Make just the interactive button a client component, not the whole page.

cta: Which *component* did you make client-side?
caption:
A whole page marked as client code is a common habit.
Keep the interactive parts small and the rest on the server.
Do you default to server components yet? 👇

hook: Freelancing includes *sales*, whether you like it or not

points.title: Finding clients is part of the work
points.body: Nobody hands you projects just because your code is good.

points.title: Good code does not market itself
points.body: People must know you exist and understand what problem you solve for them.

points.title: Small habits beat occasional bursts
points.body: A little outreach each week is easier than panicking when work dries up.

cta: What part of *selling* do you dislike?
caption:
Most of us became developers to build, not to pitch.
But selling is what keeps the building going.
What part of finding clients is hardest for you? 👇

hook: Open your proposal with *their* problem, not your bio

points.title: Read the job post twice
points.body: The second read shows details and goals you missed the first time.

points.title: Restate the goal in your own words
points.body: It proves you understood what they need before you talk about yourself.

points.title: End with one specific question
points.body: A sharp question about their project shows real thought and invites a reply.

cta: What *opening* line works for you?
caption:
Clients skim dozens of proposals. Make yours about them.
Lead with their problem, then explain how you would help.
How do you start your proposals? 👇

hook: A database *transaction* means all steps succeed or none do

points.title: Some changes must happen together
points.body: Moving money means taking from one account and adding to another. Both, or neither.

points.title: Roll back if anything fails
points.body: If one step errors, the database undoes the earlier steps as if nothing happened.

points.title: Commit only when everything worked
points.body: Only then are the changes saved and visible to everyone else.

cta: Where would a *transaction* protect you?
caption:
Without transactions, half-finished changes can leave data broken.
All or nothing keeps your data trustworthy.
Have you used transactions in your projects? 👇

hook: Someone *paying* is stronger proof than someone praising

points.title: Compliments cost people nothing
points.body: Saying your idea is great is easy. Handing over money is not.

points.title: A pre-order shows real need
points.body: Even a small early payment tells you the problem matters enough to solve.

points.title: Deliver it by hand first
points.body: You can do the work manually for early customers before you build anything automatic.

cta: Would you *charge* before building?
caption:
Likes and kind words feel good but prove very little.
Payment, even a small one, is the clearest signal.
Have you ever asked for money before building? 👇

hook: Keep a *setup checklist* for every new project you start

points.title: List the steps you always repeat
points.body: Repo, environment variables, linting, database, and deployment are usually the same each time.

points.title: Fewer decisions means faster starts
points.body: You skip the small choices and get straight to building the real thing.

points.title: Update it after every project
points.body: Add what you forgot and remove what you never used. It improves over time.

cta: What is on your *checklist* first?
caption:
Starting projects from memory wastes energy.
A simple checklist makes day one calm and repeatable.
What is the first item on yours? 👇

hook: Keep *secrets* out of every AI prompt you write

points.title: Never paste keys or passwords
points.body: API keys and .env values do not belong in a chat with any AI tool.

points.title: Swap in placeholders instead
points.body: Replace real values with fake ones like YOUR_API_KEY. The AI still understands the code.

points.title: If one leaks, rotate it
points.body: Treat a pasted secret as exposed. Create a new key and disable the old one.

cta: Do you *check* before you paste?
caption:
It is easy to paste a whole file without thinking.
A quick scan for secrets can save you a lot of trouble.
Do you scan before you paste? 👇

hook: Turn on *RLS* before your Supabase table goes live

points.title: Without RLS, tables can be too open
points.body: Tables exposed through the API can be read by anyone holding your public key.

points.title: Policies decide who sees which rows
points.body: Write rules like users can only read rows that belong to them.

points.title: Test as a real user and as anon
points.body: Try both. Confirm the right people get data and everyone else gets nothing.

cta: Which *table* needs a policy first?
caption:
Row level security is your safety net in Supabase.
Turn it on early, then write policies as you build.
Do you test your policies as an anonymous user? 👇

hook: Saying *no* to the wrong project protects your time

points.title: Unclear goals cause endless rework
points.body: If the client cannot explain what success looks like, the project rarely ends cleanly.

points.title: Every yes costs you something
points.body: Taking a poor-fit job means less time for better work and less energy overall.

points.title: A polite no keeps doors open
points.body: Explain briefly, suggest another option if you can, and stay friendly.

cta: When did you last say *no*?
caption:
Turning down work feels risky, especially early on.
But the wrong project can cost more than it pays.
What red flag makes you say no? 👇

hook: Split work into *milestones* so both sides stay covered

points.title: Smaller deliverables are easier to agree on
points.body: Each milestone has a clear description of what done looks like.

points.title: Payment follows real progress
points.body: Both sides know what is finished and what is paid at every stage.

points.title: Problems show up early
points.body: Misunderstandings appear after one milestone, not at the very end of the project.

cta: How do you *split* your projects?
caption:
Big projects with one final payment create stress for everyone.
Milestones keep expectations clear and progress visible.
How many milestones do you usually set? 👇
